演奏者通常站立於鑼旁，左手以拇指與其餘手指夾持鑼上緣邊框，右手持一端包覆軟質材料: The player usually stands beside the gong, gripping the upper rim with the thumb and the rest of the fingers of the left hand while the right hand strikes the boss with a short beater padded at one end; a beginner can practise striking and damping with a single beater first, pressing hand, knee or beater against the boss after the stroke to control the ring. With two gongs, an assistant can hold the low gong at an angle and damp it by hand; one player can also take both, or two players can take one each. Begin with a steady beat and complementary left-right rhythms, then add variations.

阿貢鑼由兩面垂直懸掛的寬邊鑼組成，較大者音高較低，較小者音高較高且較厚，在合奏中: The agung consists of two wide-rimmed gongs hung vertically; the larger is lower in pitch, the smaller is higher and thicker, and it provides the bass of the ensemble. The sound is deep and loud, and pressing hand, knee or beater against the boss after the stroke gives a firm note that decays quickly; an assistant can hold the low gong at an angle and press its face to control the ring. Compared with the gandingan the agung has a smaller diameter but a rim that curves further inward, and there is a further technique of striking the face of the gong to draw a metallic sound.
阿貢鑼的發聲體為大型、厚重、寬邊鑼，來源指出依所用金屬不同，重量可從約五磅至二三: The sounding body of the agung is a large, heavy, wide-rimmed gong; the source notes that the weight varies with the metal used, from about five pounds to twenty or thirty, commonly thirteen to sixteen; the metals include bronze, brass or iron. It is struck with a beater made from a short wooden stick whose end is wrapped in a soft but tough material such as rubber. It is hung with rope from a beam, a ceiling, a branch or a gong stand. The source does not state the materials of the other parts.
阿貢鑼的起源被認為在印尼，名稱源自馬來語 agong 與印尼／爪哇語 ageng: The agung is thought to come from Indonesia, and the name derives from Malay agong and Indonesian/Javanese ageng. In the 1770s the British explorer Thomas Forrest recorded that the people of the Philippines prized round-bossed gongs from Cilegon in Java. It later became an accompanying instrument of the kulintang ensemble among the Maguindanao, Maranao, Sama-Bajau and Tausug peoples of the southern Philippines, and spread to Palawan, Panay, Mindoro, Mindanao and to Sabah, Sulawesi, Sarawak and Kalimantan, forming an important part of the agung orchestra.
阿貢鑼見於菲律賓馬京達瑙、馬拉瑙、薩瑪-巴瑤與陶蘇格人的庫林當合奏，作為低音支持: The agung is heard in the kulintang ensembles of the Maguindanao, Maranao, Sama-Bajau and Tausug of the Philippines as the low supporting instrument, alongside the gandingan gongs, the babandil gong and the dabakan drum; it is also used in the agung orchestras of Palawan, Panay, Mindoro, Mindanao, Sabah, Sulawesi, Sarawak and Kalimantan. Beyond ensemble playing it can be used in solo competitions, in tagunggo pieces, to call a sultan's council, to mark the hours during Ramadan, and to strike the balubalu rhythm when earthquakes come.

阿貢鑼（Agung）是菲律賓傳統鑼類樂器，H-S編號111.241.2，由兩面寬: The agung is a traditional Philippine gong, H-S 111.241.2, made up of two wide-rimmed, vertically hung pot-shaped gongs, the larger low in pitch and the smaller high. The player strikes the central boss with a short beater, and it is usually paired with the babandil gong, the gandingan gongs and the dabakan drum. It serves as the supporting instrument in the kulintang ensembles of the Maguindanao, Maranao, Sama-Bajau and Tausug, and also appears in the agung orchestra.
